records.sourceFile: An overview of blood flow restriction physiology and clinical considerations.pdf

paper.citation: Martin PM, Bart RM, Ashley RL, Velasco T, Wise SR. An Overview of Blood Flow Restriction Physiology and Clinical Considerations. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2022;21(4):123-128.
paper.abstract: Blood flow restriction (BFR) has attracted attention for strength enhancement, muscle hypertrophy and improved function in specific populations. BFR creates a hypoxic environment within a muscle group that stimulates protein synthesis, satellite cell gene regulation and fibre recruitment. Consideration of the individual patient, occlusion pressure, cuff width and cuff size is paramount. BFR is described as consistently safe and effective for augmenting rehabilitation of the upper and lower extremities.
paper.tldr: Low-load BFR can build strength and muscle in rehabilitation when cuff pressure is set as a percentage of occlusion pressure and the athlete is screened. It gives smaller strength gains than heavy loading, so its main value is when heavy loads are not tolerated.
paper.methods: A narrative overview of BFR physiology (metabolic stress, mechanical tension, cell swelling, cardiovascular responses, hyperemia), protocol choices (occlusion pressure, cuff width and material, load selection), alternative uses (passive BFR, aerobic BFR, older adults) and safety (VTE, rhabdomyolysis, oxidative stress, numbness). The paper describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria.
paper.findings: Low-load BFR (about 30% of 1RM) produced hypertrophy and strength gains, and a meta-analysis found greater strength gains than repetition-matched low-load training but less than heavy training. Recommended pressures ranged from 40% to 80% of arterial occlusion pressure, with one study finding 40% effective and higher pressures possibly giving no added benefit; in a survey of 250 practitioners, only 11.5% set pressure as a percentage of occlusion pressure. A reported Kaatsu VTE incidence of 0.06% was below the general population rate in Japan, and one group estimated rhabdomyolysis at 0.07% to 0.2% in published studies and 0.008% in Japan, while another argued that muscle damage risk, mainly with protocols taken to failure, should not be overlooked.
paper.limitations: The paper is a narrative overview with no search method, so study selection cannot be judged. Protocols and cuff methods varied across the cited studies, and the authors state that mechanisms are not fully understood and that more research is needed on the contribution of each pathway. Safety statements depend partly on incidence figures from one country, and the authors note disagreement over cardiovascular risk in patients with hypertension, heart failure or peripheral arterial disease.
paper.practicalImplications: When heavy loading is not tolerated during rehabilitation, low-load BFR at about 30% of 1RM with cuff pressure set as a percentage of the individual's occlusion pressure (40% to 80%, with 40% possibly sufficient) may be used, with cuff width and size matched to the limb. Screen for the listed contraindications, VTE risk factors and cardiovascular risk first, and avoid taking low-load BFR to failure, given the damage concerns raised.
paper.athleteDev: Limited but relevant. The review reports strength and hypertrophy gains with low-load BFR, aerobic gains with BFR walking or cycling, and smaller strength gains than heavy loading. Athlete performance benefits are not tested in trained athletes, so the paper supports BFR as a supplement when heavy loading is limited, not as a replacement for heavy training.
paper.rtp: Relevant to rehabilitation, where the review describes BFR as an option for postoperative and injured patients who cannot tolerate heavy loads. It does not give return-to-sport criteria or timing, and it cannot be used to show that BFR shortens return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Blood Flow Restriction Training for        Postoperative Lower-Extremity Weakness- A Report of Three Cases.pdf

paper.citation: Tennent DJ, Burns TC, Johnson AE, Owens JG, Hylden CM. Blood Flow Restriction Training for Postoperative Lower-Extremity Weakness: A Report of Three Cases. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2018;17(4):119-122.
paper.abstract: This case report describes three highly active patients who still had muscle atrophy and weakness after arthroscopic knee surgery despite a full course of therapy. Each then completed supervised blood flow restriction training. The paper prints no separate abstract, so this summary is taken from its Introduction and results.
paper.tldr: Three patients with persistent knee weakness after arthroscopic knee surgery gained isokinetic strength after 2 to 4 weeks of supervised BFR training at 30% of 1RM. With three uncontrolled cases, this is a feasibility signal, not proof that BFR beats standard rehabilitation.
paper.methods: Three patients with persistent quadriceps or hamstring weakness after arthroscopic knee surgery (one female collegiate athlete and two male active-duty soldiers) completed supervised BFR training. Three exercises were performed at 30% of 1RM with cuff pressure at 80% of limb occlusion pressure, four sets to failure with 30 s rest, for 2 weeks (patient 1) or 4 weeks (patients 2 and 3); session frequency is not reported. Isokinetic peak torque and total work at 90 degrees per second were measured before and after training.
paper.findings: Peak torque deficits at 90 degrees per second fell in all three patients. Final knee extension deficits were 53.37%, 14.28% and 29.82%, and final knee flexion values were 11.66%, a 63.33% surplus over the uninvolved limb, and 27.08%. The authors report average relative peak torque gains of 51% (flexion) and 50% (extension) and total work gains of 190% and 108%, with no statistical testing.
paper.limitations: Three uncontrolled cases with no comparison group, no statistics and only isokinetic outcomes. All patients had completed prior physical therapy, so time and other rehabilitation effects cannot be separated from BFR. Some table values look implausible (patient 2 flexion total work up 398.5%, and peak torque labelled in joules), and the authors state that well-controlled trials are needed.
paper.practicalImplications: For athletes with persistent quadriceps or hamstring weakness after knee surgery who have stalled on standard rehabilitation, a supervised low-load BFR block could be a trial option, with isokinetic or equivalent strength testing before and after. The paper does not support routine use or superiority over heavier loading.
paper.athleteDev: Limited. The paper reports strength changes in three injured patients, one of them a collegiate athlete. It does not measure sport performance in trained athletes, so any performance benefit is an extrapolation.
paper.rtp: Relevant as a possible adjunct when knee weakness persists after surgery. Patient 1 returned to recreational running and sport-specific training one month later, patient 2 to unrestricted running and his Army fitness test, and patient 3 only to the start of straight-line running, but there is no comparator or return-to-sport criteria. The paper cannot show that BFR shortens return to sport or lowers reinjury risk.

records.sourceFile: Current implementation and barriers to using blood flow restriction training - Insights from a survey of allied health practitioners.pdf

paper.citation: Scott BR, Marston KJ, Owens J, Rolnick N, Patterson SD. Current implementation and barriers to using blood flow restriction training: insights from a survey of allied health practitioners. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2023.
paper.abstract: An online survey of allied health practitioners working with clinical or older populations asked how they prescribe BFR exercise and what prevents others from using it. Of 397 analysed respondents, 308 had prescribed BFR, mostly for musculoskeletal rehabilitation, with pressure set relative to occlusion pressure and low-load resistance or aerobic exercise. Non-users cited lack of equipment, insufficient education and safety concerns, and a follow-up survey of 22 non-users suggested affordable, convenient education.
paper.tldr: Practitioners who use BFR mainly apply it in musculoskeletal rehabilitation with occlusion-pressure-based cuffs and low-load protocols such as the 30-15-15-15 scheme, largely in line with published guidelines. Muscle soreness is commonly reported, and lack of equipment and training are the main reasons others do not use it.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional online survey (Qualtrics, 38 questions in 8 sections) advertised from April 2021 to February 2022 through social media, email and professional newsletters, with a follow-up survey of non-users from June to August 2022. Of 520 who consented, 397 provided usable data; 27 of 72 non-users who agreed to follow-up completed it, 5 had since started BFR and 22 answered barrier questions. Free text was content-analysed, and chi-squared tests examined associations between demographics, BFR use and side effects.
paper.findings: Users most often aimed BFR at muscle strengthening (86.4%), injury rehabilitation (83.4%) and hypertrophy (78.2%), and 21.4% worked mainly in a sporting environment. Resistance BFR most often used 20 to 39% of maximum load, 4 sets in a 30-15-15-15 scheme, 30 to 45 s rest and 2 to 3 days a week, and 60.2% used automatic tourniquet systems. Of 269 responders on side effects, 65.8% reported delayed-onset muscle soreness and none reported myocardial infarction or rhabdomyolysis; 84% would prescribe BFR for clients with grade 1 hypertension, alone or with medical clearance.
paper.limitations: Self-selected respondents and prewritten answer options may bias results, and free-text questions had lower response rates and were hard to categorise. Responses came mostly from physiotherapists and North America. Two authors run BFR education companies. The Results report lower-body pressures 'primarily in the range of 60-80% AOP' while the Discussion says 50 to 80%. The PDF prints 2023, while the Crossref record gives 2024; the PDF year is used here.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners using BFR should screen for contraindications such as clotting disorders, deep vein thrombosis history and previous stroke, set pressure from a measured occlusion pressure, and introduce BFR gradually to limit muscle soreness, as the authors recommend. The authors advise caution with hypertensive clients even though most respondents would treat them.
paper.athleteDev: The survey describes rehabilitation and clinical practice, not athlete training outcomes, so it does not show whether BFR improves athletic performance. It can help performance staff compare their BFR parameters with common practitioner practice.
paper.rtp: Rehabilitation staff can use the reported prescription and screening norms as a practice benchmark when adding BFR to injury rehabilitation. The study measured no clinical outcomes, so it cannot inform return-to-play timing or criteria.

records.sourceFile: Effects of photobiomodulation on pain and return to play of injured athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Morgan RM, Wheeler TD, Poolman MA, Haugen ENJ, LeMire SD, Fitzgerald JS. Effects of photobiomodulation on pain and return to play of injured athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(6):e310-e319.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated photobiomodulation (PBM) for musculoskeletal pain and time to return to play in injured athletes. Six randomised controlled trials, including 205 competitive and recreational athletes with a mean age of 24 years, were included. PBM reduced pain compared with control groups (SMD 1.03, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.63, p=0.0089). The two trials on time to return to play did not support a benefit of PBM.
paper.tldr: In injured athletes, photobiomodulation reduced pain more than control treatments across five small randomised trials. The two trials that measured return to play did not show a benefit, so the pain result should not be read as proof that PBM speeds return to play.
paper.methods: Systematic search of MEDLINE Complete, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, PubMed, Web of Science and Embase, with secondary searches to 7 November 2023, supplemented by reference lists and Google Scholar. Included studies were English-language peer-reviewed randomised controlled trials in athletes aged 18 to 44 years reporting pain or return to play after injury, screened independently by two reviewers with a third resolving disagreements. Quality was rated with the PEDro scale (Cohen's kappa 1), pain effects were pooled with a random-effects model in Meta-Essentials, and return-to-play data were summarised narratively.
paper.findings: Six trials published between 2004 and 2022 were included, with PEDro scores of 6 to 10; five contributed pain data, and the pooled pain effect favoured photobiomodulation (SMD 1.03, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.63, p=0.0089, I2 46.9%). Of the two return-to-play trials, one found a shorter return with an aloe-based gel than with photobiomodulation (about 8 vs 11 days), and the other found no difference between photobiomodulation and placebo (about 23 to 24 days in each group).
paper.limitations: The Abstract and Results say six RCTs were analysed, but only five trials measured pain (the sixth, Medeiros et al., measured return to play) and the Discussion and Limitations state the meta-analysis had five studies. The aloe comparator gel also contained arnica, devil's claw and tocopherol, and the hamstring trial was powered only for large effects. Heterogeneity was moderate, the protocol was not registered, injury severity was not reported, and small samples limit precision.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians working with injured athletes may use photobiomodulation as an adjunct to reduce pain, with devices of 810 to 980 nm as in the included trials. The authors suggest 3 to 10 minutes per application, 3 to 4 times per week, for at least 3 to 8 weeks, but this dosing was not tested in the meta-analysis. It should not be expected to shorten time to return to play.
paper.athleteDev: This review does not assess performance outcomes in healthy athletes, so it does not support photobiomodulation as a way to improve training or competition performance. Its findings apply to pain management in injured athletes.
paper.rtp: The pain findings can inform symptom management during rehabilitation. The two return-to-play trials, with different comparators and no pooled estimate, showed no clear benefit, so the review cannot be used to set or shorten return-to-play timelines.

records.sourceFile: Exertional Heat Stroke, the Return to Play Decision, and the Role of Heat Tolerance Testing- A Clinician’s Dilemma.pdf

paper.citation: O'Connor FG, Heled Y, Deuster PA. Exertional heat stroke, the return to play decision, and the role of heat tolerance testing: a clinician's dilemma. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2018;17(7):244-248.
paper.abstract: Exertional heat stroke is a leading preventable cause of morbidity and mortality in athletes and warfighters. Because a prior event is an important risk factor, return to play or duty decisions after heat stroke are difficult. This special communication reviews current guidance and evidence on these decisions and the potential role of heat tolerance testing, which exposes a person to a controlled heat load to assess heat tolerance.
paper.tldr: Return to play after exertional heat stroke has no evidence-based guideline. The authors suggest combining history, clinical biomarkers and, where indicated, a heat tolerance test, which has useful but limited diagnostic data.
paper.methods: Special communication. A clinical case is used to frame the problem. The authors review ACSM return-to-play recommendations, US and French military recurrence studies, and the Israel Defense Force heat tolerance test protocol and results. No systematic search is described.
paper.findings: ACSM guidance is summarised as at least 7 days without exercise after release, follow-up tests at about 1 week, a gradual 2-week return in a cool environment, and a laboratory heat tolerance test if vigorous activity is not reached within 4 weeks; in a large US Army cohort, a prior serious heat illness was associated with 4.02 times the odds of a later mild event. In an IDF study, 6 of 145 soldiers tested after heat stroke had a recurrent heat illness (4 of 35 classified heat intolerant, 2 of 110 heat tolerant), only one of which was heat stroke and occurred in a heat-tolerant soldier, giving reported sensitivity, specificity and accuracy of 66.7%, 77.7% and 77.2%. The test is a 120-minute treadmill walk at 5 km/h and 2% incline in 40 degrees C, with intolerance defined by rectal temperature above 38.5 degrees C, heart rate above 150 bpm, or no plateau.
paper.limitations: Selective narrative with no systematic search or quality appraisal, and the authors state their conclusions are a collective opinion. The HTT criteria come from young, moderately fit soldiers and are not adjusted for sex, aerobic capacity, training, acclimatisation or body fat. The recurrence and accuracy data come from a single military population and describe heat illness mostly as heat exhaustion, not heat stroke. The PDF prints 2018, matching Crossref.
paper.practicalImplications: After exertional heat stroke, ACSM guidance as summarised here is to rest at least 7 days, recheck affected organs at about 1 week, and return gradually over about 2 weeks in a cool environment. Clinicians should combine history, biomarkers and functional observations, and consider a laboratory heat tolerance test if the athlete has not returned to vigorous activity within 4 weeks, interpreting it in light of the test's population and adjustment limits.
paper.athleteDev: The article does not address performance training. Its heat tolerance test criteria were set for young, moderately fit soldiers and are not adjusted for fitness or acclimatisation, so it gives no guidance on heat training for healthy athletes.
paper.rtp: This article is directly about return-to-play decisions after exertional heat stroke. It supports gradual reintroduction with follow-up testing, and the authors regard a successful heat tolerance test as a reliable tool when used within a broader decision process, while stating that data are insufficient to support it as a stand-alone diagnostic test and that no evidence-based guideline exists.

records.sourceFile: Testing Limb Symmetry and Asymmetry After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury - 4 Considerations to Increase Its Utility.pdf

paper.citation: Jordan MJ, Bishop C. Testing limb symmetry and asymmetry after anterior cruciate ligament injury: 4 considerations to increase its utility. Strength and Conditioning Journal. 2024;46(4):406-414.
paper.abstract: The limb symmetry index is widely used to judge recovery after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury, but the evidence supporting it for return-to-sport decisions is mixed. The authors outline four considerations for improving its use, including benchmark choice, task-dependent movement asymmetry, movement strategy, and an envelope-of-function approach.
paper.tldr: Do not rely on a single limb symmetry percentage after ACL injury. Pair it with a benchmark that suits the athlete, measure both limbs across several tests and movement strategies, and judge readiness against the sport's demands.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the scientific literature on limb symmetry and asymmetry indices after ACL reconstruction, with practical considerations drawn from that literature. No systematic search or quantitative synthesis is described.
paper.findings: The authors argue that the postinjury contralateral limb is a poor default benchmark because ACL injury can reduce its strength and function, which can inflate the LSI. Movement asymmetries are often variable and task-dependent, and a performance-based LSI can hide a different movement strategy, since stronger hip extensors can let an athlete match jump distance while masking knee-extensor weakness. They propose using preinjury or noninjured control benchmarks where available, measuring several tests and movement cycles, and tracking both limbs across a sport-specific envelope of function.
paper.limitations: No search method is described, so the selection of evidence cannot be checked. The authors state that the evidence on LSI cut-offs and reinjury is mixed, and that longitudinal biomechanical testing and load monitoring for return to sport are in their infancy. Preinjury baseline data and control groups are often unavailable in clinical or community settings, which limits the benchmarks they propose.
paper.practicalImplications: Keep the LSI as one measure rather than the only return-to-sport criterion. Use preinjury or control benchmarks where data exist, and read the contralateral limb with caution after ACL injury. Test several tasks over several trials and sessions, check reliability for the asymmetry measures you use, and track each limb's own performance over time.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the paper supports tracking both limbs independently across vertical and horizontal jumps, change-of-direction tasks and strength tests, with jump strategy measures such as countermovement and drop-jump kinetics alongside the symmetry ratio. Compare the athlete with the demands of the sport and the planned load, not with a single symmetry percentage.
paper.rtp: The paper supports a multi-test, both-limb approach to return-to-sport readiness after ACL reconstruction, but it does not supply validated pass or fail thresholds. Do not use it to replace LSI cut-offs such as 85 or 90 percent with a new number, because the envelope-of-function approach has no threshold yet.
